Thinking recycling solves all waste. Reduce and reuse come first; many plastics are not actually recycled.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 quiz: 1) First NSPE canon: hold paramount public safety, health and welfare. 2) Tacoma Narrows: aeroelastic flutter in a slender, flexible deck. 3) Challenger: O-ring failure in cold; managers overrode engineers. 4) FOS = failure load ÷ working load; 1,500 N ÷ 500 N = 3. 5) Life cycle stages: raw materials, manufacturing, distribution/transportation, use, end of life (disposal/recycling). 6) Cradle to cradle = designing products so materials can be fully reused/recycled at end of life. 7) Utility patent lasts 20 years from filing. 8) Trademark protects brand names/logos and can last indefinitely if used and renewed. 9) Copyright protects creative works (generally the author's life + 70 years). 10) Prior art = existing evidence that an invention is already known. Mastery 8+/10.

days.guide: Map a water bottle's life cycle: raw materials (petroleum → PET), manufacturing, transportation, use, disposal (landfill, recycling, litter). Estimate impacts at each stage.

questions.q: What are the main stages of a product's life cycle?
questions.a: Raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution/transport, use, and end of life (disposal or recycling).

questions.q: Which stage of a single-use water bottle likely has the biggest impact?
questions.a: Material production/manufacturing and end of life (plastic waste) — use has almost no impact since it's used briefly.

days.guide: Redesign a disposable product for disassembly and recycling: single material, snap fits instead of glue, labeled plastics, refillable parts.

questions.q: Why does using a single type of plastic help recycling?
questions.a: Mixed materials are hard or impossible to separate; a single labeled material can be recycled together.

days.guide: Compare patents, trademarks, copyrights and trade secrets with examples.

questions.q: Which IP protects the Coca-Cola recipe? The Nike swoosh? A new type of hinge? A song?
questions.a: Trade secret; trademark; patent; copyright.

questions.q: How long does a U.S. utility patent last?
questions.a: 20 years from the filing date (with maintenance fees).

days.guide: Search Google Patents for prior art on a product idea; read one patent's abstract and first claim.

questions.q: What are a patent's 'claims'?
questions.a: The numbered statements that define exactly what the patent legally protects.

questions.q: What is prior art?
questions.a: Any public evidence (patents, products, publications) that an invention already exists, which can prevent a new patent.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 quiz in the key.

questions.q: What is 'cradle to cradle' design?
questions.a: Designing products so that at end of life their materials become inputs for new products, rather than waste.

weeks.prep: Review the student's engineering notebook for space. Help line up potential users to interview (family, neighbors, a community group). Have a decision matrix template and Gantt chart template (spreadsheet) ready.
misconceptions: Picking a problem that is too big ('solve homelessness') or has no real user. Scope to something buildable in 8 weeks with a specific user.
Choosing a solution before defining the problem. The problem statement must not contain the solution.
Unrealistic schedules. Build in time for rework and testing; the prototype rarely works the first time.
weeks.assessment_key: Design brief rubric: 4 = names a real client/user; problem statement describes the need without implying a solution; at least four measurable criteria and three constraints (budget, time, materials/tools, size, safety); justification from user interviews; 3 = all parts, criteria partly unmeasurable; 2 = solution embedded or missing constraints; 1 = incomplete. Gantt chart: pass when it covers weeks 28–36 with research, ideation, CAD, build, testing, report and presentation tasks, durations, dependencies and at least one buffer.

days.guide: The student lists 15 problems noticed at home or in the community, then picks three candidates based on interest and feasibility.

questions.q: What makes a good capstone problem?
questions.a: A real user with a real need, a problem small enough to prototype and test in about 8 weeks with available tools and budget.

days.guide: Interview at least two potential users for each candidate; record quotes.

questions.q: Why interview users before choosing a problem?
questions.a: To confirm the problem is real and important to them, and to learn needs that will shape criteria.

days.guide: Select the problem with a weighted decision matrix (impact, feasibility, user access, interest, cost).

questions.q: Weights: impact 3, feasibility 2. Problem A scores 4 and 3; problem B scores 5 and 1. Which wins?

days.guide: Write the design brief: client, problem statement, criteria, constraints.

questions.q: Rewrite 'Design a phone app that reminds Grandma to take pills.' as a solution-neutral problem statement.
questions.a: 'Grandma sometimes forgets whether she has taken her daily medications, which risks missed or double doses.'

days.guide: Submit the design brief and a Gantt chart for weeks 28–36; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why include buffer time in a Gantt chart?
questions.a: Problems and delays always happen; buffer keeps the final deadline achievable.

weeks.prep: Help the student access library databases (public library card) and Google Patents. Have a benchmarking table template ready.
misconceptions: Skipping existing products. If a cheap product already solves the problem well, the design needs a clear improvement.
Writing specifications that can't be tested ('easy to use'). Specifications need numbers and test methods ('a first-time user can open it in under 10 seconds').
Citing unreliable sources. Use manufacturer data, standards, textbooks, patents and reputable articles.
weeks.assessment_key: Research summary rubric: 4 = benchmarking table of five existing solutions (price, key features, weaknesses) with sources; summaries of two related patents (number, title, what it claims, how the design differs); technical principles explained (e.g. levers, friction, heat transfer, circuits) with sources; at least five measurable specifications each linked to a criterion with a test method; citations in a consistent format; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing patents or specs; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Benchmark five existing solutions in a table: price, features, weaknesses (from reviews).

questions.q: What is benchmarking?
questions.a: Studying and comparing existing products to learn their strengths and weaknesses and set targets for a new design.

days.guide: Search Google Patents; summarize two related patents.

questions.q: What three things should you record from each patent?
questions.a: The patent number and title, what its claims protect, and how your design is different.

days.guide: Research the scientific or engineering principles the solution will depend on and note sources.

questions.q: Why research technical principles before designing?
questions.a: So the design is based on how things actually work (e.g. forces, materials, heat) and avoids predictable failures.

days.guide: Turn criteria into measurable specifications with target values and test methods.

questions.q: Turn 'the organizer should be sturdy' into a specification.
questions.a: Example: 'Holds 2 kg on each shelf with less than 2 mm sag, tested with weights over 5 trials.'

days.guide: Submit the research summary with citations; score with the rubric.

questions.q: What's the difference between a criterion and a specification?
questions.a: A criterion is a goal (sturdy); a specification is a measurable, testable target (holds 2 kg with < 2 mm sag).

weeks.prep: Have sketch paper, isometric paper, sticky notes and a decision-matrix template. Print the SCAMPER prompts (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify/Magnify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse/Rearrange).
misconceptions: Judging ideas during brainstorming. Defer judgment: quantity first, evaluate later.
Developing only one concept. Developing three forces comparison and often combines strengths.
Weighted matrices where weights don't reflect the brief. Weights should come from the most important criteria in the design brief.
weeks.assessment_key: Concept selection rubric: 4 = at least 20 documented ideas (including SCAMPER variations); three annotated isometric concept sketches with key dimensions and materials; recorded user feedback on each; weighted decision matrix with weights tied to the brief and scores justified; clear presentation of the chosen concept and why; 3 = all parts, thin justification; 2 = fewer than three concepts or no user feedback; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Brainstorm at least 20 ideas in timed rounds, then use SCAMPER on existing products for more.

questions.q: Apply SCAMPER 'Combine' to a backpack and a lamp.
questions.a: Example: a backpack with a built-in LED light for walking at night (any reasonable combination).

days.guide: Develop three concepts into annotated isometric sketches with materials and key dimensions.

questions.q: What should annotations on a concept sketch include?
questions.a: Key dimensions, materials, how parts move or connect, and how it meets the criteria.

days.guide: Show the user the three concepts; record their reactions and preferences.

questions.q: Why get user feedback before choosing a concept?
questions.a: The user may value different features than the designer expects, preventing wasted work on the wrong concept.

days.guide: Select a final concept with a weighted decision matrix.

questions.q: Concept X scores 4, 3, 5 on criteria weighted 3, 2, 1; Concept Y scores 3, 5, 4. Which wins?
questions.a: X: 12 + 6 + 5 = 23; Y: 9 + 10 + 4 = 23 — a tie; revisit with user feedback or an added criterion.

days.guide: The student presents the selected concept and justification.

questions.q: What evidence best justifies your choice?
questions.a: Matrix scores tied to the brief's criteria plus specific user feedback.

weeks.prep: Ensure Onshape access; review assembly and drawing tutorials. Help the student find supplier sites (hardware store, McMaster-Carr, Amazon) for BOM pricing.
misconceptions: Modeling purchased parts in detail. Simplify standard parts (screws, hinges) or use Onshape's standard content.
No clearance between mating parts. Add clearance for printed or hand-made parts (often 0.2–0.5 mm for 3D prints).
BOM without quantities or sources. Every line needs item, quantity, material/part number, source and cost.
weeks.assessment_key: Design review checklist: 4 = all custom parts modeled with constrained sketches; assembly with appropriate mates and no interference; dimensioned working drawing for each custom part with title block; BOM with item numbers, quantities, materials, sources, unit and total costs within the budget constraint; 3 = minor omissions; 2 = missing drawings or BOM; 1 = incomplete. During the review, ask the student to explain one design decision and one risk.

days.guide: Model all custom parts.

questions.q: What clearance might you add between a 3D-printed pin and hole?
questions.a: Roughly 0.2–0.5 mm, depending on the printer — test with a small sample.

days.guide: Assemble with mates and check interference.

questions.q: What does an interference check reveal?
questions.a: Places where parts overlap and couldn't physically fit together.

days.guide: Create dimensioned working drawings for each custom part.

questions.q: What must every working drawing include?
questions.a: Necessary views, all dimensions, tolerances/notes and a completed title block.

days.guide: Create a BOM with sourcing and cost.

questions.q: Three hinges at $2.49 each and 12 screws at $0.15 each. Total?

days.guide: Hold a design review; score with the checklist.

questions.q: What is a design review?
questions.a: A formal check of a design by others to catch errors and risks before building.

weeks.prep: Purchase materials per the BOM. Set up a safe workspace with ventilation, a first-aid kit and safety glasses. Supervise any power-tool use, and confirm makerspace print bookings.
misconceptions: Measuring once and cutting. 'Measure twice, cut once' — mark from the working drawing and check before cutting.
Skipping safety steps when rushed. Every step in the fabrication plan lists hazards and PPE.
Not tracking costs and hours. Logging against the BOM and Gantt chart shows whether the project is on track.
weeks.assessment_key: Build log check: 4 = fabrication plan with step-by-step operations, tools, hazards and PPE per step; dated progress photos; critical dimensions checked with calipers and recorded against drawing tolerances; hours and costs logged versus BOM; updated Gantt chart; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing plan or measurements; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Write the fabrication plan: each step, tools, hazards, PPE.

questions.q: For cutting plywood with a handsaw, list hazards and PPE.
questions.a: Hazards: cuts, splinters, flying dust, unstable workpiece. PPE/controls: safety glasses, clamp the work, gloves for handling rough stock (not near spinning tools), dust mask if dusty.

days.guide: Set up the workspace, mark stock from drawings and cut.

questions.q: What does 'measure twice, cut once' prevent?
questions.a: Wasted material and time from cutting to the wrong size.

days.guide: Fabricate the main structure and check critical dimensions with calipers.

questions.q: A part should be 50.0 ± 0.5 mm and measures 50.7 mm. Pass or fail?
questions.a: Fail — 50.7 is above the 50.5 mm upper limit.

days.guide: Send parts to a makerspace printer or hand-fabricate.

questions.q: What is a jig?
questions.a: A custom guide or holder that positions the workpiece or tool so operations are repeatable and accurate.

days.guide: Photograph progress, log hours and costs, update the Gantt chart.

questions.q: You're 2 days behind. What are your options?
questions.a: Use buffer time, reduce scope of nonessential features, work extra sessions, or reorder tasks.

weeks.prep: Gather fasteners, adhesives (follow ventilation labels), sandpaper/files and calipers. Keep the CAD model open for updates.
misconceptions: Forcing parts that don't fit. Measure the clearance, find which part is out of tolerance, and rework it.
Forgetting to update CAD after changes. The as-built model and drawings must match the real prototype.
Final assembly with permanent adhesive before testing. Dry-fit and use removable fasteners when possible until testing is done.
weeks.assessment_key: Assembled prototype and as-built update: 4 = all parts finished with safe edges; fit-check table of clearances vs. tolerances; reworked parts documented; CAD and drawings updated to match changes (revision noted in title block); prototype assembled and operates as intended; notebook entry explains problems and solutions; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = CAD not updated or prototype not functional; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Finish remaining parts; deburr and sand edges.

questions.q: Why deburr metal or plastic edges?
questions.a: Burrs are sharp and can cut users; removing them also improves fit.

days.guide: Dry-fit all parts, measure clearances, and record any out of tolerance.

questions.q: What does dry-fitting mean?
questions.a: Assembling parts temporarily without glue or permanent fasteners to check fit.

days.guide: Rework or reprint out-of-tolerance parts and update the CAD model.

questions.q: A printed hole is 0.3 mm too small. Give two fixes.
questions.a: Drill or ream it to size, or enlarge the hole in CAD (compensate for printer shrinkage) and reprint.

days.guide: Assemble the full prototype and verify it works.

questions.q: What does 'integration' mean in a build?
questions.a: Bringing subsystems together and making sure they work properly as a whole.

days.guide: Submit the as-built update and notebook entry.

questions.q: What is an as-built drawing?
questions.a: A drawing updated to show the product exactly as it was actually built, including changes made during fabrication.

weeks.prep: Have the prototype, measurement tools and a spreadsheet. Arrange time for the user to try the prototype. Print the specification list from Week 29.
misconceptions: Testing only what works. Test every specification, especially the riskiest.
Leading the user during user testing. Give the task, then observe silently.
Claiming success without data. Each specification needs pass/fail evidence from repeated trials.
weeks.assessment_key: Test report rubric: 4 = test procedure per specification with pass/fail criteria; at least five trials each in a spreadsheet with mean and standard deviation; user-test observations with quotes and pain points; at least one evidence-based improvement; retest data and a summary table showing each specification met or not; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = few trials or no retest; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Write a test procedure for each specification with pass/fail criteria.

questions.q: Write pass/fail criteria for 'opens in under 10 seconds'.
questions.a: Pass if a first-time user opens it in less than 10 s in at least 4 of 5 trials (or mean < 10 s); fail otherwise.

days.guide: Run five or more trials per test; compute mean and SD in the spreadsheet.

questions.q: Times: 8, 9, 7, 12, 9 s. Mean?

days.guide: The user tries the prototype while the student observes and records quotes and pain points.

questions.q: Why stay silent while the user tests?
questions.a: Explaining hides real usability problems the user would face alone.

days.guide: Make at least one evidence-based improvement.

questions.q: What makes an improvement 'evidence-based'?
questions.a: It addresses a specific failure seen in test data or user observations.

days.guide: Retest and summarize which specifications are met.

questions.q: Why retest after changing the design?
questions.a: To confirm the change fixed the problem without creating new ones.

weeks.prep: Have a word processor and a free website builder (Google Sites works well). Collect renderings, drawings, build photos and test graphs into one folder.
misconceptions: Writing the executive summary first. Write it last, as a short summary of the whole report.
Using vague words ('pretty strong'). Use technical terms and data ('held 3.2 kg, SD 0.2 kg').
Missing citations for research, images or patents.
weeks.assessment_key: Technical report and portfolio rubric: 4 = report of 2,000+ words with executive summary, problem, research, concept selection, design (drawings/renderings), build, testing (tables and graphs with data), conclusions/recommendations and citations; correct technical vocabulary; figures numbered and captioned; portfolio page publicly viewable with renderings, drawings, build photos, test graphs and a short project summary; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing sections or data; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Outline the report sections.

questions.q: What belongs in an executive summary?
questions.a: A brief overview of the problem, solution, key test results and conclusions — readable on its own by a busy reader.

days.guide: Write the full draft with figures and data tables.

questions.q: How should figures be labeled?
questions.a: Numbered with a caption (e.g. 'Figure 3. Load test results over five trials'), and referred to in the text.

days.guide: Build the digital portfolio page.

questions.q: What should a portfolio show a college or employer?
questions.a: The problem, process, visuals of the design and build, test evidence, and what the student learned.

days.guide: Revise for clarity and terminology; check every source is cited.

questions.q: Replace 'the stand was pretty strong' with technical language.
questions.a: 'The stand supported a 300 g load with no measurable deflection across five trials.'

days.guide: Submit the report and publish the portfolio.

questions.q: Why put test data in an appendix?
questions.a: Full raw data supports the report's claims while keeping the main text readable.

weeks.prep: Invite a panel (family, community members, ideally an engineer). Prepare the room with a screen and table for the prototype. Prepare a written final exam covering the course from the key below. Bookmark California community college engineering pathways (ASSIST.org for transfer) and UC/CSU engineering program pages.
misconceptions: Reading slides aloud. Slides show visuals and data; the presenter explains.
Defensive answers in Q&A. Treat questions as feedback; it's fine to say 'I didn't test that — here's how I would.'
Assuming there is one path to engineering. Community college transfer (ASSIST.org, transfer agreements) and 4-year admission are both strong routes.
weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (4 levels): 4 = about 10 minutes; covers problem, user, research, concept selection, design, build, test data and next steps; live prototype demo; clear visuals; confident Q&A; 3 = complete but uneven; 2 = missing test data or demo; 1 = unprepared. Final exam representative key: 1) Design process steps. 2) Criteria vs. constraints. 3) Isometric axes at 30°. 4) Third-angle view placement (top above front, right side to right). 5) Tolerance 12 ± 0.05 → 11.95–12.05. 6) Accuracy vs. precision. 7) Mean/SD calculation (e.g. 4, 6, 8 → mean 6, SD 2). 8) Density = mass/volume. 9) Extrude, revolve, shell definitions. 10) Revolute mate leaves 1 DOF. 11) Injection molding for high volume; 3D printing for prototypes. 12) Stiffness vs. strength. 13) 5th–95th percentile design. 14) First NSPE canon. 15) Patent vs. trademark vs. copyright. Mastery 12+/15. Pathway plan: complete if it names at least one community college and one university program, required math/science courses (calculus, physics, chemistry), and transfer or admission steps.

days.guide: Build a 10-minute slide deck; rehearse twice with a timer.

questions.q: What should the first minute of the presentation cover?
questions.a: The problem and the user — why the project matters.

days.guide: Present to the panel and demonstrate the prototype.

questions.q: What should you do if the prototype fails during the demo?
questions.a: Stay calm, explain what failed and why, and show test data or a video of it working.

days.guide: Write responses to panel questions and list next steps for development.

questions.q: Name two next steps if the product were developed further.
questions.a: Examples: test with more users, choose materials for manufacturing, reduce cost, file a provisional patent.

days.guide: Research California engineering pathways and write a plan.

questions.q: What website shows which community college courses transfer to UC/CSU?
questions.a: ASSIST.org.

questions.q: Which high school courses best prepare for engineering?
questions.a: Math through calculus, physics, chemistry, and courses in CAD/programming.

days.guide: Give the written final in the key.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a factor of safety?
questions.a: To make sure a design can carry more than the expected load, covering uncertainty in loads, materials and manufacturing.
